$comment: Apogee's scenario pool. Owned here: nothing reads a benchmark file to find out what a season is made of. A scenario is identified by the exact name KovaaK's uses, because that is what the player launches and what the leaderboard is keyed on. Edit this file to change the pool, then re-run sample:leaderboards and build:season. npm run validate:pool holds it to every claim made below.
$windows: A window is a difficulty band, and a scenario's band is the hardest tier any source publishes it in - see `bands`. Hardest rather than first, because a scenario Voltaic calls Intermediate and snakbox calls Hard is being asked for more by snakbox, and the ladder has to grade it at the harder ask or the rank it sets is one anybody in the harder band already holds. The previous pool placed each scenario by hand and the placement was a sentence in this comment rather than a rule; validate:pool now derives the window from `bands` and refuses a variant that disagrees with it.

ladder.$comment: Percentiles from the top of each scenario's KovaaK's leaderboard, one array per window, easiest rank first. Read them as ONE sequence of sixteen, not as four ladders: they must fall from the first rank to the last, across the window handovers as well as inside a window. A family is graded on the best of its variants, so a player holds the highest rank any window gives them - and a rank whose percentile is not below every rank above it is reached by nobody, because whoever reaches it reaches a higher one at the same time. Letting a handover step back is the mistake this file keeps making. The cut before this one opened Intermediate at 44.9% where Novice closed at 43.8%, and repeated Advanced's four numbers verbatim for Expert, which left ranks 13 to 16 unreachable by construction. The cut before THAT had the same fault at two handovers. npm run distribution is what catches it: it sweeps the population through the real engine and names every rank nobody holds. This ladder is checked against it and skips none. The step back is not imaginary - a player does sit at a worse percentile on a harder board, so the same ability is a larger share there - but the sweep grades a player at one percentile on every board and cannot see it. Measuring the real step needs Apogee's own population, which is season 2's job. Until then the ladder descends. The cut before this one was also far too loose, which is a different fault and was found by playing it: a high-intermediate player topped out at rank 12 - the ceiling of Advanced - on 17 of the 22 families, and reached rank 15 on one. Sixteen ranks that a mid-ladder player finishes are sixteen ranks that mean nothing. What was wrong was the range, not the shape. A KovaaK's board is mostly people who played a scenario once, so a share of it is a much weaker claim than it sounds, and the old ladder ended at the top 1.4% - which npm run calibrate places at Voltaic's Nova, three ranks short of its last. Its whole Advanced window, 32% to 15%, sat inside Voltaic's *Intermediate*. This cut is anchored on the two references that survive conversion: Voltaic S5 holds a 1.1x to 2.2x spread across scenarios at each of its thresholds and Aimerz+ S1 a 1.2x to 2.2x across its Easy tier, tight enough that both really are percentile ladders in disguise, and both land their last rank at the top 0.1%. The sixteen below are the geometric mean of those two curves, read at sixteen evenly spaced positions along each. The same history that finished the old ladder now peaks at rank 12 with a median family at 9, which is what a high-intermediate player should read. Only the last window is not the reference's own shape. Both references end at the top 0.1%, and this pool cannot: validate:pool asks that seventy players sit above a window's hardest rank, the thinnest Expert board in the pool carries 9,878 entries, and 70/9,878 is the top 0.71%. So the last rank asks the top 0.8% - the limit with enough margin that a resample does not break it - and ranks 13 to 16 are spread geometrically from where Advanced closes. That is a real ceiling and not a preference: a finer cut than this would be a fact about fewer than seventy people. The four are close together in percentile and still a normal rank apart in score, because the top of a board is steep - about 2% of score per rank, which is what Voltaic's top ranks are worth too. Then the easy end was cut again, and the reason is a measurement this pool can make and the references cannot. The windows are stacked as one descending sequence on the theory that a harder scenario draws a stronger population, so the same player sits lower on its board. The corpus on this machine says that effect is small: the same history sits at a median top 10.0% across the Novice variants it has played, 12.9% across Intermediate, 13.0% across Advanced and 17.5% across Expert - under 2x from end to end, against a ladder that asked 86% at the bottom and 0.8% at the top. So the first eight ranks were not grading anybody. They closed at the top 22%, which that history cleared on every Novice scenario it had played and 13 of 15 Intermediate ones, most of them on one to five runs. The easy end is compressed to 86/72/56/42 and 31/22/15/10.5, which drops those 13 to 6. Ranks 13 to 16 are deliberately not touched: Air Voltaic's board saturates near the top - the whole top 2.2% of it spans ten points of score - so the four Expert ranks are already only 0.45% of score apart there, and a tighter cut puts a rank step under run-to-run noise. Maxing the Novice window is not a fault this can fix and is not trying to: a window a decent player does not clear is a window that never hands over.

$matchWindow: Which window a ranked match draws its three scenarios from. Intermediate: novice scenarios stop separating two players who can both max them, and expert ones ask a first-week player to play something they cannot score on at all.
$subCategories: Eleven, derived rather than chosen: data/subskills.json normalises the category names all 43 committed benchmarks publish for their own scenarios and counts how many name each one. Nine are Voltaic's, and the derivation reproduces Voltaic's published mapping on all 106 of their scenarios, which is what makes the same treatment of everybody else's believable. Two are not Voltaic's and are named by benchmarks their sheet cannot see: Micro Clicking by eight, Reading Tracking by seven. Named in two words the way snakbox, Avasive, wobin and Aimerz+ name them, rather than as the bare word, because the bare word does not survive being read on its own - 'Micro' and 'Speed' mean different things in different categories, and a weakness map or a queue name showing one word cannot say which. Regenerate with npm run build:subskills; do not hand-edit either file's classification.
$sources: Every benchmark the pool may draw a scenario from, and nothing else. This replaces the old rule - 'the fifteen most-played benchmarks on evxl' - which could not reach Viscose, Jade Palace, Lemon Static or snakbox however good their scenarios are, and let in nothing from outside the list however good it is. Each of these is a benchmark evxl lists, has a committed definition under data/benchmarks/, and contributes at least one scenario; validate:pool checks all three. Two absences are deliberate. Avasive S2 is not here because it cannot be: its 96 scenarios carry 26 leaderboard entries between the largest of them, so no percentile cut from one of its boards describes anything. e1se Tracking Routine is not here because it is a routine rather than a graded ladder - its 'Intermediate' tier holds Voltaic Novice scenarios, and banding by it would drag the easiest scenarios in the pool two windows up.
$bands: Which window each source's difficulty tiers belong to. One row per tier rather than one per scenario, because a tier is what its author graded as a unit and 76 hand placements is 76 chances to put a Novice scenario in the Expert band - which samples fine, builds fine, and produces four top ranks anybody clears in one run. The two judgements worth naming: Voltaic's Elite tier is window 3 but is never used, because every Elite board is under 5,000 entries and a rank cut from the top 1.4% of one would be whatever two players happened to score; and Aimerz+, Revosect S1, Jade Palace and snakbox's hardest tiers are read as sitting above Voltaic's Advanced, which is the one claim here their authors did not make. npm run distribution is what checks it - a band placed too high leaves ranks nobody holds.

1w2ts reload smallflicks Entry.why: Viscose files this lineage under Micro at Easier, Medium and Hard and under Stability at Entry. One tier of one benchmark disagreeing with three of its own is a slip in their sheet rather than a different scenario: it is a two-target smallflicks wall at every tier. Without this, Micro Clicking has one lineage - the whole corpus holds exactly one other novice-tier micro scenario.

$subCategoryOverrides: Scenarios whose derived sub-skill the pool deliberately disagrees with. Each carries its reason, and validate:pool prints every one and refuses an override that agrees with the derivation anyway - an override that has stopped doing anything is a claim nobody is checking. Keep this near-empty: the derivation is right far more often than a hand edit, and the whole point of deriving it was that hand-deriving was measurably wrong on 6 of Voltaic's 18.
$families: A sub-skill is what a rank is cut on; a family is one lineage inside it, measured at four difficulties. How many families a sub-skill carries is not fixed. It used to be exactly two, written down as a rule and enforced by nothing, and it decided which scenarios could be in the pool before anything was asked about whether they train anybody - which is the wrong order for a benchmark whose job is improvement. Pick the scenarios that teach the sub-skill, then count them. What the old rule was protecting still holds and is now printed rather than forbidden: category energy is the sum of its families, so an uneven count IS a weighting - a sub-skill with three families outweighs one with two by half again. That is a legitimate thing to choose and a bad thing to fall into, so validate:pool prints the count per sub-skill every run. The four variants follow one scenario lineage wherever a lineage spans the bands - eth Pasu Micro Entry through Easier and Medium, then Anima's 1w3ts Pasu Perfected Micro Goated - and hold the sub-skill where none does. Every family's sub-skill is checked against what the benchmarks publishing its scenarios call them, so a family cannot be named Precise Tracking and quietly filled with reactive scenarios.

source.why: 31 made rank 13 exactly as hard as rank 12. tamTargetSwitch Smooth Easy asks 38 for rank 12 and 2.00% of its board clears that; tamTargetSwitch Smooth Hard asked 31 for rank 13 and 2.00% of its board cleared that too. A family is graded on the best of its variants, so everybody reaching rank 12 reached rank 13 in the same run and rank 12 was held by nobody. 32 clears about 1.67%, which puts the ladder back in order. Season 1 shipped this. The percentile ladder it was cut from descended correctly - Advanced closed at 0.03 and Expert opened at 0.022 - so the check that read the ladder saw nothing wrong. These are small integer scores, 35-38 against 31-35, and rounding a percentile onto them collapsed two ranks onto one difficulty. Measuring what share of the board actually clears each authored number is what found it.
